```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)

library(lab4)
library(mlbench)
library(caret)
```

# 1. Introduction

This vignette demonstrates ridge regression using the `ridgereg()`
function from `lab4`. We compare ordinary linear regression,
forward variable selection, and ridge regression using a held-out
test set.

# 2. Prepare the data

We use the Boston Housing dataset provided by `mlbench`.

```{r data}
data("BostonHousing", package = "mlbench")

housing <- BostonHousing
housing <- housing[complete.cases(housing), ]

set.seed(123)
train_index <- caret::createDataPartition(
  housing$medv,
  p = 0.8,
  list = FALSE
)

train <- housing[train_index, ]
test <- housing[-train_index, ]

nrow(train)
nrow(test)
```

# 3. Ordinary linear regression

```{r linear-model}
linear_model <- lm(medv ~ ., data = train)

linear_predictions <- predict(linear_model, newdata = test)
```

# 4. Forward selection

We start with an intercept-only model and use forward selection
with AIC to choose predictors.

```{r forward-selection}
null_model <- lm(medv ~ 1, data = train)
full_model <- lm(medv ~ ., data = train)

forward_model <- step(
  null_model,
  scope = list(
    lower = formula(null_model),
    upper = formula(full_model)
  ),
  direction = "forward",
  trace = 0
)

forward_predictions <- predict(forward_model, newdata = test)
```

# 5. Tune ridge regression using 10-fold cross-validation

We compare multiple penalty values using only the training data.
Each fold acts as a validation set once.

```{r ridge-cv}
x <- model.matrix(medv ~ ., data = train)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
y <- train$medv

# Tune ridge regression using 10-fold cross-validation

lambda_grid <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100)

set.seed(123)
folds <- caret::createFolds(train$medv, k = 10, list = TRUE)

# Expand the formula explicitly to avoid problems with "."
predictor_names <- setdiff(names(train), "medv")
ridge_formula <- stats::reformulate(predictor_names, response = "medv")

cv_rmse <- sapply(lambda_grid, function(lambda) {
  fold_errors <- sapply(folds, function(validation_rows) {
    fold_train <- train[-validation_rows, , drop = FALSE]
    fold_valid <- train[validation_rows, , drop = FALSE]

    model <- ridgereg(
      ridge_formula,
      data = fold_train,
      lambda = lambda
    )

    predictions <- predict(model, newdata = fold_valid)

    sqrt(mean((fold_valid$medv - predictions)^2))
  })

  mean(fold_errors)
})

cv_results <- data.frame(
  lambda = lambda_grid,
  CV_RMSE = cv_rmse
)

print(cv_results)

best_lambda <- cv_results$lambda[which.min(cv_results$CV_RMSE)]
print(best_lambda)
```



# 6. Fit the final ridge model

```{r final-ridge}

ridge_model <- ridgereg(
  ridge_formula,
  data = train,
  lambda = best_lambda
)

ridge_predictions <- predict(ridge_model, newdata = test)

```

# 7. Compare test-set performance

We use root mean squared error (RMSE). Smaller values indicate
better predictive accuracy on this test set.

```{r comparison}
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
}

results <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "Ordinary linear regression",
    "Forward selection",
    "Ridge regression"
  ),
  Test_RMSE = c(
    rmse(test$medv, linear_predictions),
    rmse(test$medv, forward_predictions),
    rmse(test$medv, ridge_predictions)
  )
)

results[order(results$Test_RMSE), ]
```

# 8. Discussion

The model with the lowest test RMSE performed best on this particular
split. Ridge regression shrinks predictor coefficients to reduce
variance, while forward selection removes predictors according to
AIC. Ordinary linear regression retains all predictors without a
ridge penalty.

The best method depends on the dataset, the split, and the penalty
chosen during cross-validation. Test data are used only for final
evaluation, not for selecting the penalty.
